title: The Picture Advantage
description: Why pictures beat words: Standing's 10,000 photos, dual coding and the learning-styles myth
tryIt: Ask someone to read out ten random objects from around the house, turn each into a picture as you hear it, then name as many as you can an hour later.

concepts.title: How it works: the picture advantage
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a challenge to make your eyes water. Someone shows you a photograph every five seconds until you have seen 10,000 of them. Days later they show you pairs of pictures and ask which one of each pair you saw before. Surely you would just be guessing?

In 1973 Lionel Standing, a psychologist at Bishop's University in Quebec, ran exactly that test. He assembled 11,000 photographic slides1 and compared ordinary photographs, especially vivid ones and single words picked at random from a dictionary. Every item was shown once, for five seconds. At 10,000 pictures the viewing took five days, at 2,000 slides a day, and Standing, who checked it on himself, called the effect extremely grueling and unpleasant.2 Yet people later picked out the picture they had seen with about 83% accuracy.3

Words did worse than pictures at every list size, and vivid pictures did best of all. What counted as vivid? An ordinary dog went into Standing's normal pile, but a dog holding a pipe in its mouth went into the vivid one;4 an airplane was normal, a crashed plane vivid.

Standing was not the first to see this. In 1967 Shepard had tested people on 612 color pictures and 540 words, and they recognized 96.7% of the pictures against 88.4% of the words.5 Psychologists call it the picture superiority effect. Nor do you keep only a rough gist. In 2008 Timothy Brady and colleagues at MIT showed people 2,500 objects over five and a half hours.6 Afterwards they could still tell an object they had seen from the same object in a different state or pose 87% of the time.7

concepts.title: Drill: see it, do not just read it
concepts.contentHtml:
Why should pictures win? The first explanation was dual coding, the theory Paivio set out in 1971. Memory, he argued, has two separate systems, one for words and one for images.1 You tend to name a picture silently as you look at it, so a picture is stored twice, as an image and as a word, while a printed word usually gets only the verbal code. Paivio and Csapo tested the obvious prediction in 1973: ask people to form an image of each word, and the picture advantage should disappear.2 It did.

There is a rival account. Pictures look far more different from one another than printed words do, and that distinctiveness may be what memory latches onto. More recently, Tyler Ensor, Aimée Surprenant and Ian Neath gave words varied fonts, sizes, colors and capital letters, and the picture advantage in recognition disappeared.3 The argument is still open, but both theories hand you the same instruction: turn each word into a picture, and make every picture unlike its neighbors.

  1. See a particular one. Not "a dog" but one dog: its color, its size, which way it faces.
  2. Name it as you see it. Say the word silently while the picture forms, so it gets both codes.
  3. Give it one odd detail that no other item on the list shares.
  4. Stay with it for five seconds, Standing's pace, then move on.
  5. Test before you peek. Recall the list from memory first and only then check it.
Drill Picture each word for about five seconds, in order, then look away. The quiz at the end of this lesson will ask you for one of them.
  1. umbrella
  2. lobster
  3. trumpet
  4. candle
  5. bicycle
  6. pineapple
  7. anchor
  8. volcano
  9. scarf
  10. telescope

concepts.title: Myth check: visual learners
concepts.contentHtml:
If pictures are this powerful, are image tricks only for people who think in pictures?

Myth Some people are visual learners and others are auditory or verbal learners, so you learn best when teaching matches your style, and picture methods are really for the visual type.
Reality In 2008 Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork reviewed the evidence for learning styles. People will happily say how they prefer to learn, but showing that matching teaching to style helps needs a particular experiment: sort students by style, teach each group in several ways, then give everyone the same test. The reviewers found virtually no evidence for the pattern such an experiment would have to show,1 and several well-designed studies flatly contradicted the matching idea. Their verdict was that there is no adequate evidence base for using learning-styles assessments in general education.2

The picture advantage, by contrast, turns up across whole groups of volunteers rather than in a chosen type, and Paivio and Csapo's result shows that picturing words narrows the gap for anyone told to do it. Pashler's team were careful to add that many versions of learning styles have simply never been tested. Still, nothing so far says you should skip the pictures because you think of yourself as a words person.

Wait, really? Standing pushed his numbers to the edge. Vivid pictures showed so little sign of filling up that he judged their memory capacity almost limitless,3 and he extrapolated: shown a million such pictures under the same conditions, people would keep about 731,400. Brady's team, for their part, stressed that their results should not be taken to mean anyone has a photographic memory.4 What the studies do show is that your visual memory has room to spare. The rest of this course is about using it on purpose.

title: Images That Act
description: The Ad Herennium's recipe for images that stick: action, extremes, costume, mud and jokes
tryIt: Pick five dull objects on your desk, give each one an Ad Herennium makeover (action, a crown or mud, a joke), and check tomorrow morning which ones you can still see.

concepts.title: How it works: the oldest recipe
concepts.contentHtml:
Try to remember what you had for breakfast on a Tuesday three weeks ago. Now remember the day something truly strange happened in your kitchen. One of those memories has vanished and the other will last for years, and a Roman teacher knew why more than two thousand years ago.

The Rhetorica ad Herennium is a Roman handbook on public speaking, written in the first century BC and long thought to be Cicero's.1 Its third book contains the oldest memory system that survives in writing. Its author starts from everyday experience: petty, ordinary things slip from the memory, while the striking and novel stay. A sunrise is marvelous to no one, but a solar eclipse is a source of wonder because it happens seldom.2 Let art, he says, imitate nature.

So build images that will cling to memory longest. Make them as striking as possible. Use images that are not many or vague, but are doing something (in his Latin, aliquid agentes). Give them exceptional beauty or singular ugliness. Dress some in crowns or purple cloaks; disfigure others with blood, mud or red paint; add comic effects.3 Do not worry that they are made up. The things we easily remember when they are real, he adds, we remember just as easily as figments, if they have been carefully delineated.4

concepts.title: Drill: give it the treatment
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is the Ad Herennium's recipe as a routine, with two modern ingredients. In 1994 the psychologist Schmidt compared funny and plain versions of the same sentences, and the funny ones were better remembered in both free and cued recall.1 Emotion seems to work in a similar way: a 2017 review by Tyng and colleagues concluded that emotion helps information get encoded and retrieved,2 while noting that its effects on memory are not always helpful.3

  1. Make it act. A thing doing something beats a thing sitting still.
  2. Push it to an extreme. Enormous or tiny, dazzlingly beautiful or truly hideous.
  3. Dress it up or mess it up. A crown or a purple cloak; mud, blood or red paint.
  4. Make it funny. A joke you would tell a friend is a joke you will remember.
  5. Add another sense. The noise it makes, the smell, how it feels in your hand.
  6. Make it yours. Choose the version that strikes you, not one someone else finds striking.
Drill Give each of these eight dull things the full treatment, in order, about ten seconds each. The quiz will ask you where one of them came.
  1. kettle
  2. ladder
  3. goat
  4. violin
  5. mirror
  6. cactus
  7. drum
  8. sandal

Stuck on the kettle? Try a copper kettle the size of a car, wearing a crown, shrieking like a whistle while it pours hot custard all over its own spout. Ridiculous, and that is the point. Then make the ladder different again: not another giant, but perhaps something that moves, squeaks or smells.

concepts.title: Myth check: is weirder always better?
concepts.contentHtml:
Ask anyone who has read a memory book and they will say the secret is to make every image as bizarre as possible. The research answer is: sometimes.

Myth The weirder the image, the better you will remember it.
Reality Psychologists call the hoped-for boost the bizarreness effect, and it is fussy. In 1995 Mark McDaniel, Gilles Einstein and colleagues reported that bizarre images beat ordinary ones consistently when the two are mixed in the same list.1 Make the whole list bizarre and the advantage goes. A 1989 study by Zoller, Workman and Kroll at the University of California, Davis, found no advantage for pure lists,2 and found that even in mixed lists the edge was limited to short retention intervals:3 in groups tested only after 48 hours there was no sign of it. Humor behaves in a similar way. Schmidt's advantage for funny sentences was limited to experiments that mixed funny and plain sentences, although sentences people personally rated as funny were remembered better either way.4

So oddness works by contrast. A strange image stands out against ordinary neighbors, the way the Ad Herennium's eclipse stands out against daily sunsets; a list that is all strangeness is just a new kind of normal. That is why the recipe is a toolkit, not a single dial. Action, extremes, costume, comedy and the senses give you many ways to make each image unlike the one beside it.

Wait, really? You might expect a joke to lose its power if you know it is coming. In Schmidt's experiments it did not: the humor advantage persisted even when people were warned that they were about to read a funny sentence.5

title: Pictures for Ideas
description: Turning abstract words into images by sound, symbol and scene, and the Ad Herennium's rudest example
tryIt: Take five abstract words from today's news headlines and turn each into a picture by sound, symbol or scene, then see how many you can recall at bedtime.

concepts.title: How it works: concrete beats abstract
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture an elephant. Easy: gray, enormous, flapping its ears. Now picture "justice". You probably reached for something else, a pair of scales or a judge's wig, because justice itself has no shape. That little detour is the whole skill of this lesson.

Concrete words are usually remembered better than abstract ones,1 a finding called the concreteness effect. Dual-coding theory explains it the same way as the picture advantage. The chance of a word getting a second, image code falls from pictures, to concrete words, to abstract words, because people are highly likely to name a picture, somewhat less likely to picture a concrete noun, and least likely to picture an abstract one.2 The fix follows directly: find a concrete stand-in for the abstract word, and you give it the image code it was missing.

The Ad Herennium's author knew the problem. He describes two kinds of likeness,3 one for the matter of what you want to say and one for its words, and a likeness of matter can hold a whole idea in one image. His example is a lawsuit: the prosecution says the defendant poisoned a man to get an inheritance, and there were many witnesses. So picture the victim ill in bed, and the defendant at the bedside holding a cup in his right hand, tablets in his left, and on his fourth finger a ram's testicles.4

The cup is the poison and the tablets are the inheritance. The testicles are a pun: Latin testes also means witnesses, as the translator Harry Caplan explains in his notes. He adds that purses were made from a ram's scrotum, so a hint of bribe money may be in there too. Rude, vivid and doing three jobs at once: an active image by the book.

concepts.title: Drill: three bridges
concepts.contentHtml:
For words, the Ad Herennium works by sound. To remember the line Iam domum itionem reges ("And now their home-coming the kings"), it tells you to picture Domitius raising his hands to heaven while he is lashed by the Marcii Reges.1 Domitius sounds like domum itionem, and Rex was the name of one of the most distinguished families of the Marcian clan. As Caplan notes, the play is on the form of the word, not its meaning. You can use that bridge and two more.

  1. Sound. Break the word into pieces that sound like things you can picture. Gravity: a cup of tea sitting on a grave.
  2. Symbol. Use an object that already stands for the idea. Gravity: a falling apple. Justice: a pair of scales.
  3. Scene. Show someone living the idea. Gravity: you, sliding off a wet roof. Patience: an angler watching a float for a week.
  4. Take the first strong one. Do not hunt for the perfect image; the first one that makes you smile is usually yours.
  5. Then make it act, with the levers from the last lesson.
Drill Build a picture for each abstract word, in order, using any bridge. The quiz will ask which word came where.
  1. freedom
  2. envy
  3. wisdom
  4. luck
  5. danger
  6. honesty
  7. comfort
  8. ambition

concepts.title: Myth check: a picture for every word?
concepts.contentHtml:
It is tempting to imagine the ancient masters reciting whole speeches by turning every single word into a picture.

Myth Memory images are for learning things word for word, so the experts made a picture for every word.
Reality The Ad Herennium treats images for words as the harder task, and says to first go over a verse two or three times to yourself before you represent its words with images,1 so that art supplements nature. Its author says he included word memory not to get verse by rote but as an exercise to strengthen memory for matter, which is of practical use.2 The later Roman teacher Quintilian doubted that symbols could record a run of connected words at all, observing that some words, such as conjunctions, cannot be represented by images.

So use one image per idea, not one per word, and lean on plain rehearsal for exact wording. That raises a practical question: why not buy a ready-made dictionary of images and save yourself the bother? Most of the Greeks who wrote on memory, the Ad Herennium reports, had done exactly that, listing images that corresponded to a great many words.

Wait, really? The author thought those lists were ridiculous. Out of the infinite store of words, why collect images for a thousand?3 Worse, a ready-made list robs you of your own initiative, and one person is struck by one likeness while another is struck by another. His conclusion could be the motto of this course: everybody, therefore, should in equipping himself with images suit his own convenience.4

title: The Link Method
description: Chaining a list with interacting images, and why two pictures side by side can hurt
tryIt: Link your next shopping list of up to ten items into a chain of interacting images, then do the shop without looking at the list.

concepts.title: How it works: images that touch
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone reads you a shopping list: milk, eggs, bread, soap. You picture each one clearly, one after another. At the shop you remember the milk and then nothing. Your pictures were fine. What was missing was the glue between them.

In 1970 Gordon Bower and David Winzenz at Stanford gave people pairs of nouns to learn with one of four strategies: repeating the pair, reading it in a sentence, making up their own sentence linking the two, or picturing the two things in vivid interaction.1 The ranking was clear in both recall and recognition: imagery best, then making up a sentence, then reading one, with rote repetition worst.2 Their explanation was that memory benefits when you actively search out and generate a relation between two things, what they called an "actor-action-object" relation.

The link method, sometimes called the chain, turns that finding into a way to learn a list in order. You never picture an item alone. You picture item one acting on item two, then two on three, then three on four, so each image holds the cue for the next. The milk floods a box of eggs; the eggs hatch, and out march slices of bread; the bread scrubs itself clean with a bar of soap. Recall the first image and the chain pulls out the rest.

The weakness is built in: everything hangs on the links. Forget one, and every item after it loses its only cue. Keep that in mind, because the next lesson, and the palace in the next skill, both answer it.

concepts.title: Drill: forge the chain
concepts.contentHtml:
Interaction is the whole game, so this routine is mostly about how two images meet.

  1. Make the first item unforgettable. Nothing comes before it, so give it the full treatment from Lesson 2.
  2. Work in pairs. Only ever think about two items: the one you just placed and the next.
  3. Make one act on the other. Actor, action, object: a hammer flattens a strawberry, not a hammer lying next to a strawberry.
  4. Let go of the old pair. Once a link feels solid, drop the earlier item and link the newest one to the next.
  5. Repair weak links straight away. If a pair feels thin, make the action bigger before you go on.
  6. Read it back both ways. Start at the first item and ask what it was doing to the next one, then try from the end.
Drill Link these ten items into one chain, about ten seconds a pair, then cover the list and read the chain back. The quiz will ask you to put some of them in order.
  1. rocket
  2. banana
  3. piano
  4. penguin
  5. ladder
  6. teacup
  7. lighthouse
  8. sock
  9. wheelbarrow
  10. kite

If a link snapped, find where. Very often it is a pair you pictured side by side instead of making one do something to the other. The myth check shows why that matters so much: separate images are not just a wasted chance.

concepts.title: Myth check: side by side
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a belief that sounds harmless: as long as each picture is vivid, it does not matter how you arrange them.

Myth Two vivid pictures held in mind side by side will remind you of each other.
Reality In 1972 Keith Wollen, Andrea Weber and Douglas Lowry pulled apart the two things memory books recommend, bizarreness and interaction. People learned pairs of words while seeing pictures of the two things either interacting or not, and either bizarre or ordinary; a control group saw only the words. Bizarreness made no difference to recall.1 Interacting pictures beat the words-only group, but pictures of the two things apart did worse than no pictures at all.2

So a non-interacting image is not neutral; it can get in the way. The rule for your chain is simple: if the two things are not touching, colliding, eating or wearing each other, you have not made a link yet.

Wait, really? Bower and Winzenz's ranking hides a second surprise. Making up your own sentence beat reading a ready-made one, even though both linked the same two words. Their account was that your memory benefits from actively searching out, discovering and generating the relation yourself.3 The effort of inventing a link is part of what makes it stick, which is one more reason to build your own images rather than borrow someone else's.

title: The Story Method
description: Weaving a list into a story: Bower and Clark's 93 percent, and memory without a mind's eye
tryIt: Turn tomorrow's to-do list into a two-minute story with yourself as the hero, then retell it at lunchtime and tick off what it reminds you of.

concepts.title: How it works: one story per list
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone gives you ten words to remember. Then another ten, and another, until you have had twelve lists. You recall each list perfectly just after you learn it. Then, at the end, they test you on all twelve again. How much is left?

In 1969 Gordon Bower and Michal Clark at Stanford ran that study. One group used narrative chaining: they made up a meaningful story woven around each list of ten nouns, taking as long as they needed, typically one to two minutes.1 Each storyteller was paired with a "yoked" control who got exactly the same time to study the same list by normal study and rehearsal. Straight after each list, everyone's recall was perfect.2 But at the final test on all twelve lists, the storytellers recalled six or seven times as much: a median of 93% of the words against 13%.3

Why such a gulf? Bower and Clark pointed to three things a story does. It organizes the list around a theme.4 It keeps the twelve lists from blurring into one another, which psychologists call reducing interference. And at recall it guides reconstruction: even if a word slips, the plot tells you what kind of thing must come next. That makes a story sturdier than a chain. Each link joins only two items, so one broken link strands the rest, while a plot runs through the whole list and can carry you over a gap.

concepts.title: Drill: tell yourself a story
concepts.contentHtml:
A story is a chain with a reason behind every link. Here is how to build one.

  1. Read the list once to see what you are dealing with.
  2. Pick a hero. You, or someone you know well, so every scene has a point of view.
  3. Make each word the next event, in order, and make each event cause the one after it.
  4. Keep the scenes active with the levers you already know, but let the plot do the heavy lifting.
  5. Take your time. Bower and Clark's storytellers took one to two minutes for ten words.1
  6. Tell it once from start to finish, then pull the words back out of the story.
Drill Weave these ten nouns, in order, into one story in about two minutes, as Bower and Clark's storytellers did. The quiz will ask you for some of them.
  1. wizard
  2. bucket
  3. motorway
  4. parrot
  5. chocolate
  6. iceberg
  7. saxophone
  8. castle
  9. pillow
  10. tractor

When you test yourself, notice what happens at a gap. Instead of drawing a blank, you can ask what the hero needed next and why, and the missing word often walks back in. That is reconstruction at work, and it is why a story forgives the occasional slip that would break a chain.

concepts.title: Myth check: no pictures in your head?
concepts.contentHtml:
Close your eyes and picture a red apple. Some people see it vividly, some see something faint, and some see nothing at all.

Myth If you cannot see pictures in your mind's eye, image methods cannot work for you.
Reality Being unable to form voluntary visual images is called aphantasia, and the lifelong, congenital form is thought to affect around 2% of people.1 In 2021 Bainbridge and colleagues asked 61 people with aphantasia and matched controls to draw real scenes from memory. The aphantasic group recalled significantly fewer objects, but placed them just as accurately, made fewer memory errors and leaned more on words.2 As one participant put it: "I have to store the pieces as words.3" Notice too that Bower and Clark asked for a meaningful story, not a vivid film. Plot, sound, place and meaning are all codes you can use. These studies do not settle how well image methods work for people with aphantasia, so try them, and keep what works.

Wait, really? The particular system may matter less than you think. In 2000 Wang and Thomas tested people's memory for word lists after a delay. Those who spontaneously used organizing or imagery strategies of their own did about as well as people trained in the method of loci and the pegword technique.4 The storytellers' controls in Bower and Clark's study had exactly the same time, spent on normal study and rehearsal. The difference was what each group did with it.

A story still has a weak spot: you need the plot to find anything, and you cannot jump straight to item seven. The next skill fixes that by giving every image an address of its own.
